title: Overlap system set executions
body:
## What problem does this solve or what need does it fill?

Imagine an app with two systems, A and B, who don't have any conflicting resource accesses. System A is scheduled in system set X, and system B is scheduled in system set Y. The system sets are ordered (X, Y).chain().

Execution for A and B is currently done serially, even though there's nothing in theory disallowing overlap between them.

The render world heavily uses system sets to order execution, as otherwise it would be very difficult to always manually specify that bind_foo systems need to run after prepare_a, prepare_b, prepare_c, etc.

However this leads to unfortunate gaps where we have idle threads waiting for a few final systems to finish before starting the next system set:

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/7160af4d-33d6-4967-b8e8-cc7fc09cd3f0)

The caveat is dependencies that Bevy can't track, such as interior mutability on read-only component/resource accesses, or global variables.


## What solution would you like?

Allow execution of systems in different system sets to overlap.

## What alternative(s) have you considered?

Rework the render world to not use system sets.

reporter
comments.body:
The problem is that it would be a _lot_ of dependencies if we had to manually specify every system ordering. It would break really easily and be hard for 3rd party plugins to extend.

I'd be fine if we made this an optional mode, but I do think it's the best solution we have.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
Okay, fair enough. I think I visualize the problem more clearly now.

Maybe something like
```rust
let (my_prepare, my_bind) = app.clone_sets((Prepare, Bind));
```
which would maintain the relationships between the sets. So the user knows that `my_bind` *will* run after `my_prepare`, but *can* run at the same time as any other `Prepare`.

Though it's still an extra line of code for every group of systems, so might still be a headache.

In general though, I'm no longer opposed to this, but I do think it needs to be optional.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
I'm not sure what the clone_sets() API would do in your proposal. Can you elaborate?

I was thinking we could add an `IntoScheduleConfigs::chain_loose()` method, and use that when setting up RenderSystems.

```rust
// Current
schedule.configure_sets(
    (
        ExtractCommands,
        PrepareMeshes,
        ManageViews,
        Queue,
        PhaseSort,
        Prepare,
        Render,
        Cleanup,
        PostCleanup,
    )
        .chain(),
);

// Proposed
schedule.configure_sets(
    (
        ExtractCommands,
        PrepareMeshes,
        ManageViews,
        Queue,
        PhaseSort,
        Prepare,
        Render,
        Cleanup,
        PostCleanup,
    )
        .chain_loose(),
);
```

comments.author: participant3
comments.body:
> The caveat is dependencies that Bevy can't track, such as interior mutability on read-only component/resource accesses, or global variables.

tbh if these are the only caveats, then I struggle to find a reason why it shouldn't be the default. Would users even be able to observe a difference?

If you use those kind of features that sidestep usual bevy workflow you can either create a marker `Res` and use it in your systems to force ordering, or switch to "`strict systemset ordering`" (current impl).

Calling this mode loose or weak sounds like it's bad somehow. What about overlapping, greedy, eager, packed, or something more along those lines.

What I'm more curious about is if there are scenarios where you want this overlapping mode but for some reason want to opt-out for a specific system set or system 🤔 .

comments.body:
I also have a lot of `.chain()` calls in my projects. I am aware that some of them are possibly independent. In terms of what ECS brings to the table, I find it difficult to support a case where the "bevy knows better" behavior is not the default. The following is all opinion posting, no facts-at-hand here:

ECS is all about separation of concerns. It are those disparate pieces, one cohesive product, that makes it all worthwhile. From my code-design perspective, It is extremely powerful to focus solely on this separation than it is to ever be concerned with the perfect system ordering. I want to get it "just good enough" so that bevy can handle find the scheduling optimizations of which I was never aware. I want my hand to be held. This is why I love using rust. I do not want to make up for the scheduler's lack of enthusiasm for things it knows could be better. Therefore, I support that if a system must be run in its explicit sequence, in complete adherence to my wishes, that I should be opting out of a default hand-holding scheduler.

Nonetheless this sounds awesome :)

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
> How does this work with commands? Does bevy somehow know what systems spawn which entities, and therefore needs flushing and an ordering constraint before running a system in another set for when we add chain_loose?

Bevy currently assumes that any system that emits commands and is ordered before another system needs a command flush between it and the next system. You can override that assumption, but that's the default :) 

I would expect chain_loose to work the same way here, with `Commands` being treated as a wildcard "could mutate anything" bit of metadata.

comments.author: participant8
comments.body:
> Imagine an app with two systems, A and B, who don't have any conflicting resource accesses. System A is scheduled in system set X, and system B is scheduled in system set Y. The system sets are ordered (X, Y).chain().
>
> Execution for A and B is currently done serially, even though there's nothing in theory disallowing overlap between them.

But when the user or someone else says "these sets need to be chained" then there must be a reason for this? The sets should not be chained in the first place if it really does not matter.

For example [a system in my crate has no world access at all](https://github.com/participant8/bevy_oozlum/blob/8a0e8478319391c0bef5391c39313da663b0c73d/src/schedule/system.rs#L502). The purpose of it is to queue undoing commands at the right time. It is absolutely important that it is possible to be ordered by the `BackwardDeferredSet`/`BackwardDeferredAndSystemSet` sets, otherwise my reversible scheduling impls will not work. (see the [parent module](https://github.com/participant8/bevy_oozlum/blob/8a0e8478319391c0bef5391c39313da663b0c73d/src/schedule/mod.rs) and search for the set usages).

> I would expect chain_loose to work the same way here, with Commands being treated as a wildcard "could mutate anything" bit of metadata.

If this parallelization only affects systems without commands, it would be fine for my use case.

comments.author: participant9
comments.body: I strongly believe that we should keep the current `chain` the default, and then have a new `chain_weak` or something. It would be **very** confusing if you happen to be using interior mutability and suddenly the systems that were chained suddenly are running in parallel. This is fundamentally an optimization and optimizations are built on assumptions. If that assumption breaks then that optimization is invalid. In this case, a user could be doing something fairly innocuous from the perspective of Rust and then suddenly be battling system-ordering demons.

comments.author: participant10
comments.body:
Would another solution not be to make the system execution graph more expressive. Currently systemsets implicitly mean "Start at label X, must be done before the next label runs". One could make the last part configurable "Start at label X, must be done before label Y runs or frame end" (if you want to run across frames i argue one must use async). 
If the system would not be done by the time label Y is reached it effectively blocks as it does now. If it has already finished it is a trivial check and starts executing label Y.
This should result more freedom for the scheduler to schedule more systems in parallel as it sees fit.

`app.add_systems(MyStartLabel, MyEndLabel, my_system()) `or `app.add_systems(MyStartLabel, my_system().finish_before(MyEndLabel))` (if `finish_before` is not specified behavior is the current behavior, next label)


This would allow to run more things in parallel, downside:  easy to make spaghetti (default is the same as current behavior though, so opt-in) + if we can visualize the graph bugs might still be reasonable to identify.

comments.author: participant8
comments.body: The configuration could also be on the `SystemSet` derive level. It would make it harder for third-parties to opt-in or opt-out, however you do not need to search your whole code for weak chains when you just have to look at the set definition.
